findings.title: Crash recovery can restore links without restoring the running service
findings.risk: A crash after service relaunch can leave runtime/current on the previous release while the live service keeps running the failed candidate.
findings.why_it_matters: This creates the lifecycle split brain the recovery contract is meant to prevent and can mislead status and subsequent check-only operations.
findings.evidence: Recovery changes links and clears the journal without service relaunch or health acceptance; status bypasses recovery; current tests cover only link restoration.
findings.recommendation: Make recovery service-aware and health-gated under the lock, and make status reconcile or report pending recovery.
validation: Crash after service relaunch and before health is reproduced.
Next operation relaunches and accepts the restored release.
Status and check-only update cannot leave or hide a mismatched live process.

findings.agent_fix_prompt: Add the crash-boundary regression, implement service-aware journal recovery, run lifecycle, service, retention, and distribution suites, and report the exact repaired candidate.

findings.title: Lifecycle diagnostics grow without a bound and are read in full
findings.risk: Repeated lifecycle events can consume disk indefinitely and make diagnostic export synchronously load an arbitrarily large file.
findings.why_it_matters: Long-lived nodes degrade during incident recovery and the explicit bounded-diagnostics acceptance gate is unmet.
findings.evidence: The emitter only appends one JSONL file and the endpoint reads the entire file; no bound or rotation exists.
findings.recommendation: Add deterministic size-capped rotation and bounded-tail export while preserving redaction, permissions, and containment.
validation: High-volume events keep disk usage within the configured bound.
Export returns newest redacted events without unbounded reads.
Rotation is symlink-safe and remains inside the managed log directory.
